items.title: Cedar Walton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: he went to the Jazztet with uh Art Farmer and them – uh, Art Farmer and Benny Golson. But uh that uh was uh a very memorable uh nice uh high level uh of music, period, for me, being with J.J. Johnson.

ctx.x: What was his concept of orchestration?

[laughs] You want me to say that in one sentence? Or one uh month? Uh, no, it was simple uh, it was, had a certain amount of uh, uh directness to it, uh and uh, uh, he would feature himself uh of course which is what people wanted to hear when they came out to hear J.J. Johnson, the number one voted trombone player every year for that period, you know. And uh he was a very healthy man, you know. Uh, I, I, would measure a person's health by if he had all his original teeth, and he did. He's one of the few people I…
You know, I was going to, you know, since you're talkin' about J.J. and I think that other, you know the other, maybe another …

items.title: Benny Golson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Then on the 23rd we have the rehearsal... We’re going to play – the new Jazztet is going to perform... That would be Curtis Fuller, Cedar Walton, Ron Carter, Al Harewood, and me.

ctx.x: I see that big smile on your face.

That was something. Kenny Dorham, Freddie Hubbard, Jackie McLean, Benny Golson, Cedar Walton, Reggie Workman, and Roy Haynes. Boy, that was something. But Kenny was – Freddie was playing so much. I said, oh, I feel sorry for Kenny Dorham. Boy, this guy. It was unreal. And Roy Haynes, the consummate drummer. The chronology means absolutely nothing to him. I said to him, “Where do you hide your portrait?”, like Dorian Gray. The portrait gets old, but he doesn’t get old. I went to hear him at the Blue Note in New…
What was your reception like when you went to Japan?
